After the pseudocode assignment count = 7, distinguish the variable's name from its stored value.
The variable's name is count.
Its stored value is 7.
The identifier is count, and it currently holds the number seven.
The name is 7 and the stored value is the word count.
In this language, integer division discards the fractional part and real division retains it. Evaluate integer 7/2 and real 7/2.
Integer division gives 3.
Real division gives 3.5.
With integers the result is three; with real-number division it is three and a half.
Integer division gives 4 and real division gives 2.
A loop visits i = 0,1,2,3,4 but should visit exactly the first four zero-based array positions. Identify the extra index and the correct upper-bound condition.
Index 4 is the extra iteration.
The loop should require i < 4 rather than i <= 4.
It visits the fifth position by mistake; testing strictly less than four fixes the bound.
Index 0 is always invalid, so changing the condition to i <= 5 fixes it.
Here = assigns a value and == tests equality. Explain x = 5 and x == 5.
x = 5 stores 5 in x.
x == 5 checks whether x equals 5 without assigning it.
The single equals sign updates x to five; the double sign compares its existing value with five.
Both expressions always assign ten to x.
With left-to-right short-circuit AND, explain why x != null AND x.ready avoids a null dereference.
If x is null, the first condition is false.
A false first operand prevents evaluation of x.ready.
Null makes the left test fail, so short-circuiting skips the field access.
AND always evaluates both operands, but null automatically has a ready field.
A function prints 5 and then returns 8. State what appears on output and what value the caller receives.
The printed output is 5.
The function's returned value is 8.
Five is displayed, while the call evaluates to eight.
Eight is printed and the caller receives five.
A recursive function returns at n = 0; otherwise it calls itself with n - 1 for a positive integer n. Identify its base case and progress step.
The base case is n = 0.
Subtracting one moves positive n toward the base case.
Zero stops recursion, and each call reduces n by one until that stopping value is reached.
The base case is any negative infinity, and increasing n indefinitely guarantees termination.
Why can deep recursion exhaust a call stack even when it has a valid base case? Mention retained calls and finite memory.
Unfinished recursive calls retain stack frames until they return.
The available stack space is finite and can be exceeded before reaching the base case.
Each pending call occupies a frame, and too many such frames can fill the limited stack before recursion ends.
Every recursive call immediately deletes all earlier frames, and stack memory is infinite.
Contrast a function-local variable with mutable state shared by two functions.
A local variable belongs to its function's local scope.
Changes to shared mutable state can be observed by other code using that state.
A function's local binding is scoped there, whereas updating shared data can affect another function that accesses it.
Every local variable is automatically public worldwide, and shared state can never be changed.
a and b reference the same mutable list [1,2]. After appending 3 through a, state b's contents and explain why.
b observes [1,2,3].
Both references point to the same list object.
Reading b gives one, two, three because the names alias one underlying list.
b becomes an empty list because every reference automatically creates an independent copy.
Contrast shallow and deep copies of a list containing mutable inner lists.
A shallow copy duplicates the outer list while retaining references to the inner lists.
A deep copy also copies the nested mutable contents under the stated ordinary structure.
A shallow copy creates a new outer list but shares its inner lists; a deep copy makes new outer and inner lists.
A shallow copy recursively duplicates everything, while a deep copy only renames the original list.
Push A then B onto an empty stack. Which item is popped first, and what ordering rule explains it?
B is popped first.
A stack follows last-in-first-out order.
The first removal is B because the most recently pushed item leaves first.
A is popped first because a stack is first-in-first-out.
Enqueue A then B into an empty queue. Which item is dequeued first, and what ordering rule explains it?
A is dequeued first.
A queue follows first-in-first-out order.
A leaves before B because the earliest arrival is served first.
B leaves first because a queue must always be last-in-first-out.
Compare accessing position k in an ordinary random-access array and in a singly linked list starting at its head.
The array can access position k directly in constant time under the usual model.
The linked list requires following links up to that position, taking time proportional to k.
Array indexing is O(1), while reaching the same position from a list's head takes O(k) traversal.
An array must follow k linked nodes, while every linked-list position is directly addressable in constant time.
Two different keys hash to the same bucket. Define this event and explain whether one value must be lost.
This is a hash collision.
A collision-resolution method such as chaining can retain both entries.
The keys collide, but storing a chain or using another resolution scheme preserves both mappings.
This is proof the keys are identical, so one value must always be deleted.
For a conventional hash table, contrast expected lookup time with a possible worst case when many keys collide.
With suitable hashing and load, expected lookup is O(1).
A worst-case lookup can be O(n) if many entries must be examined.
Normal expected access is constant-time, but pathological collisions can make a lookup scan a linear number of entries.
Expected lookup always takes O(n squared), while the worst case is guaranteed O(0).
Why can linear search work on an unsorted list, and what is its worst-case work for n elements?
It checks elements individually without relying on ordering.
It may examine all n elements, giving O(n) worst-case work.
The search tests each candidate regardless of sort order and can scan the whole list in the worst case.
It works only on sorted input and always inspects exactly one element.
A sort orders records by age. What does stability guarantee, and what does an ordinary correct sort guarantee without that extra property?
Stability preserves the original relative order of records with equal ages.
A correct age sort places ages in the requested nondecreasing or nonincreasing order.
Stable sorting keeps ties in their previous sequence; basic sorting correctness requires the chosen age ordering.
Stability randomly shuffles equal ages, and a correct sort need not order ages at all.
During insertion sort, a sorted prefix [2,5] is followed by the next item 3. Give the new prefix and state the maintained invariant.
The new prefix is [2,3,5].
The processed prefix remains sorted after each insertion.
Inserting three produces two, three, five, maintaining the property that all processed elements form an ordered prefix.
The prefix becomes [5,2,3], and the invariant requires processed elements to remain unsorted.
Why does an O(n log n) algorithm not necessarily beat an O(n squared) algorithm on a small input? Explain asymptotic scope and a practical factor.
Asymptotic complexity describes growth as input size becomes large.
Constants and overhead can dominate runtime on small inputs.
The growth-rate notation concerns sufficiently large n; small jobs may be determined by setup costs or constant factors.
Big-O gives the exact runtime in seconds for every input and excludes all implementation overhead.
An outer loop runs n times and its inner loop always runs exactly three times. Give total inner iterations and asymptotic complexity.
There are 3n inner iterations.
The total loop work is O(n), assuming constant work per iteration.
The inner body executes three times n, so the running work grows linearly.
There are n squared iterations and the work must be exponential merely because loops are nested.
Why use a visited set when traversing a finite graph with cycles? Explain repeated visits and termination.
The set identifies vertices that have already been processed.
Skipping repeated processing prevents cycling indefinitely and allows the finite traversal to finish.
Remembering processed vertices lets the traversal avoid revisiting them forever around a cycle.
The visited set creates new vertices indefinitely and guarantees every cycle is followed forever.
In an unweighted graph, why does breadth-first search find a path with the fewest edges? Mention exploration order and equal edge costs.
Breadth-first search explores vertices in increasing distance measured in edge count.
With equal edge costs, fewer edges also means a shortest path under that cost model.
It expands one edge-distance layer at a time, and uniform edge weights make minimum edge count the desired path cost.
It follows a deepest branch first, and arbitrary unequal edge costs never matter.
A graph has a single directed edge A -> B. State reachability from A to B and from B to A using only that edge.
B is reachable from A.
A is not reachable from B using that directed edge alone.
Travel is possible from A to B, but the reverse journey has no directed path here.
Only B can reach A, because arrows always point opposite the permitted direction.
An undirected graph contains edges A-B, B-C and C-A. Identify the cycle and explain why the graph is not a tree.
A-B-C-A forms a cycle.
An undirected tree must be acyclic.
Following A to B to C and back to A closes a loop, violating a tree's no-cycle requirement.
There is no cycle, and trees are required to contain a triangle.
Contrast a primary key with a nonunique database index.
A primary key uniquely identifies a row and does not allow null key values.
A nonunique index can speed lookup without requiring indexed values to be unique.
The primary key is a unique non-null row identifier; an ordinary nonunique index is a lookup aid that permits duplicate values.
A primary key must contain duplicates, while every nonunique index prohibits all repeated values.
An orders.customer_id foreign key references customers.id. State its integrity requirement and whether a customer may exist without any referencing order.
The non-null foreign-key value must match a referenced customer key.
A customer may exist without any order referencing it.
Every non-null customer reference on an order must identify an existing customer, but a customer is allowed to have no orders.
Orders may reference nonexistent customers, and every customer must have at least one order.
Distinguish SQL WHERE from GROUP BY in a basic aggregate query.
WHERE filters individual input rows by a condition.
GROUP BY collects rows into groups used for aggregation.
WHERE selects which records remain; GROUP BY organizes the remaining records into aggregate groups.
WHERE always creates a new table schema, while GROUP BY deletes all aggregation results.
A join key appears twice in table A and three times in table B. How many matching pairs does an equality join produce for that key, and why?
It produces six matching rows.
Each of the two A rows matches each of the three B rows.
There are six pairs because the join combines every matching row on one side with every matching row on the other.
It always produces one row because joins automatically remove every duplicate key.
A transfer subtracts 10 from one balance and adds 10 to another. What does transaction atomicity require if the second step fails?
The subtraction must also be rolled back if the transfer cannot commit.
Atomicity makes the grouped operation all-or-nothing.
A failed credit must undo the debit, because the transaction's changes are committed together or not at all.
Atomicity requires keeping the debit and permanently losing the money whenever credit fails.
Two workers both read counter 5, each computes 6, then each writes 6. Give the final value and explain the lost update.
The final counter is 6.
One increment is lost because both writes were based on the same old value rather than incorporating the other increment.
It ends at six, as the second stale write fails to preserve both independent increments.
It ends at seven because stale writes automatically merge every arithmetic operation.
Does mutual exclusion alone rule out deadlock? Define its guarantee and describe how two locks can still deadlock.
Mutual exclusion prevents simultaneous access to a protected resource by competing holders.
Two tasks can deadlock if each holds a lock while waiting for the other's lock.
Exclusive access protects one resource at a time, yet circular waiting across multiple held locks can still freeze both tasks.
Mutual exclusion means all tasks share every lock simultaneously, so circular waiting is impossible by definition.
A client retries a payment-like test operation after losing the response. Explain how a duplicate effect can occur and what was uncertain.
The first request may already have completed before its response was lost.
Repeating a non-idempotent operation can apply its effect a second time.
The server may have acted on the original request despite the missing reply, so executing the retry again can duplicate the change.
A missing response proves the server did nothing, so retries can never repeat an effect.
How does an idempotency key help with two submissions of the same logical operation? State the key requirement and server behavior.
Retries of one logical operation use the same key, while different logical operations use different keys.
The server recognizes the repeated key and reuses the recorded outcome instead of applying the effect again.

Keep one identifier for retries of an operation and choose a different identifier for a different operation; the server returns the saved result for a repeated identifier without applying the change again.
Each retry must use a fresh key, which instructs the server to execute every duplicate again.
Distinguish authentication from authorization.
Authentication establishes who the requester is.
Authorization decides what that requester is allowed to do.
The first checks identity; the second checks permission for an action or resource.
Authentication means deciding disk size, while authorization means changing an unknown user's identity randomly.
Explain how parameterized SQL treats an untrusted value and whether an ordinary bound value parameter can substitute for a table name.
The input is bound as data separate from the SQL statement structure.
An ordinary bound value parameter cannot substitute for a table name or other SQL identifier.
Values are supplied separately from executable query structure; ordinary value placeholders cannot choose the table name.
Parameters paste user values directly into executable SQL, and an ordinary bound value can replace any table identifier.
Distinguish cryptographic hashing from reversible encryption.
A cryptographic hash is designed as a one-way digest rather than a reversible encoding.
Encryption is designed to recover plaintext using the appropriate key.
Hashing produces a digest without a decryption procedure; encrypted data can be decrypted with the correct key.
Every hash has a built-in secret decryption key, while encryption permanently discards all recoverable information.
Why give each stored password hash a unique salt? Explain identical passwords and precomputed attacks.
Different salts make identical passwords produce different stored hash results.
Salts prevent reuse of one precomputed hash table across all salted records.
Per-record salts distinguish equal passwords' hashes and force precomputation to account for each salt separately.
A salt is a universal secret that makes all password hashes identical and enables one lookup table for everyone.
Distinguish encryption in transit from authorization at the receiving server.
Transport encryption protects data while it travels between endpoints.
The server still needs to check whether the requester may access or change the resource.
Encrypted transport protects the communication path, while permission checks determine what the receiving application allows.
An encrypted connection automatically grants every requester administrator access and removes all need for permission checks.
Why is browser-only input validation insufficient to protect a server? Mention request origin and where enforcement must occur.
A requester can bypass the browser interface and send a custom request.
The server must validate and enforce its own required constraints.
Requests need not pass through the supplied UI, so the backend must check the rules itself.
Every possible network request is forced through the exact browser form, so servers should trust all input blindly.
Contrast a cache hit with an origin response that has just been fetched.
A cache hit serves a previously stored response or value.
A fresh origin response is obtained from the source service for that request.
The cache reuses saved content, while an origin fetch asks the source to provide a response now.
A cache hit always rebuilds the source database, while an origin response is necessarily a years-old local copy.
A source value changes from 10 to 12 while an unrefreshed cache still holds 10. State what the cache can return and why it is stale.
The cache can return 10.
Its stored copy has not been updated to reflect the new source value.
It may serve the old ten because the cached entry has not caught up with the source's change.
The cache must return 12 instantly because every cached copy updates itself without communication.
Distinguish network latency from throughput.
Latency is the delay for a communication or response.
Throughput is the amount of data transferred per unit time.
One measures how long communication takes to arrive; the other measures the sustained data rate.
Latency measures bytes per second, while throughput measures only the waiting time before the first byte.
Packets A and B are sent in that order over a generic network. Explain whether arrival order is guaranteed and how a protocol can reconstruct order.
Arrival order is not guaranteed without an ordering mechanism.
Sequence numbers can let a protocol reorder received data.
B may arrive before A; numbering the data allows the receiver to restore the intended sequence.
Every possible network guarantees send order automatically, and sequence numbers contain no ordering information.
A client times out waiting for a server operation. What does the timeout establish, and what does it leave uncertain?
The client did not receive a response within its waiting limit.
It does not establish whether the server performed the operation.
The reply was not received in time, but the server-side outcome may still be either completed or incomplete.
A timeout proves the server never received the request and guarantees no change happened.
Distinguish a text's language from its character encoding.
The language is the linguistic system, such as French or Japanese.
The encoding specifies how characters are represented as code units or bytes, such as UTF-8.
French identifies the human language; UTF-8 describes a representation of its text as bytes.
UTF-8 is a spoken language, while Japanese is a compression algorithm for bytes.
Why can a Unicode string's byte count differ from its visible character count? Mention encoding length and multi-code-point characters.
An encoding such as UTF-8 can use multiple bytes for one code point.
A visible character can consist of multiple code points, such as a base letter plus a combining mark.
Code points need not take one byte each, and a displayed character may combine several code points.
Every visible Unicode character is exactly one byte and can never contain a combining mark.
Why can binary floating-point 0.1 + 0.2 differ slightly from exact decimal 0.3? Explain representation and accumulated arithmetic effects.
Many finite decimal fractions, including 0.1, have no finite binary representation.
Operations on their rounded representations can produce a small rounding discrepancy.

Decimal 0.1 and 0.2 repeat indefinitely in binary, so finite binary floating point stores rounded approximations; arithmetic on those rounded values can leave a small discrepancy from exact decimal 0.3.
Binary floating point stores every decimal fraction exactly, and any discrepancy proves that addition has no mathematical meaning.
Why does a passing finite test suite not prove a general program correct on every input? Mention coverage and an untested case.
The tests exercise only the selected inputs and conditions.
A defect can remain on an input or path that the tests did not cover.
Success is evidence for the scenarios run, while an unexamined input may still trigger a bug.
Passing one example exhaustively covers all possible programs and guarantees there are no untested inputs.
A function returns the largest integer in a nonempty list and must reject an empty list. Name the boundary case and its required behavior.
An empty list is a boundary case.
The function must report an error or explicit rejection for that input.
Test zero elements, expecting rejection rather than a fabricated maximum.
The boundary is an ordinary long nonempty list, and an empty list must silently return an invented zero.
